name: Bush medicine taken alongside diabetes and blood pressure tablets
what_people_do: Take bush teas or herbal remedies for "sugar" and "pressure" in addition to, or sometimes instead of, prescribed medicines; about a third of Barbadian church-goers use herbal remedies.
why_they_say_it_works: Plants are "natural", familiar, cheap and passed on by older relatives.

documented_by.source: Cohall DH et al 2012, West Indian Med J, PMID 23155984
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Barbados: about 33% of Christian church-goers surveyed used herbal remedies, including for chronic conditions; health insurance made no difference to use.

documented_by.source: Mahabir D, Gulliford MC 1997, Rev Panam Salud Publica, PMID 9128111
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Trinidad: 42% of 622 diabetes patients used bush medicine; 81% of users gathered the plants themselves; insulin users were less frequent users.

evidence.tested: Drug-herb interactions: 11 popular Barbadian plants against the commonest antihypertensives
evidence.finding: 27 of 30 compounds showed strong binding to drug targets; Catharanthus roseus, Phyllanthus niruri, Petroselinum crispum and Lantana involucrata flagged. Predicts possible interactions, not proven ones.

source.name: Barbadian botanicals and antihypertensive drugs, in silico, 2022, ACS Omega, PMID 36530331

harm_note: Interaction risk is predicted (computer modelling), not observed in patients. The practical point: tell the doctor or pharmacist what you are drinking.
gaps: No clinical study of an actual interaction found.
Non-disclosure rate in Caribbean patients not found (African figure: James 2018, 55.8 to 100% do not disclose).
